summary:
Dagestan is a republic within the Russian Federation and stands under the national framework set out in Russia's own record; that layer is not restated here.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, version 2.0 of June 2025, names the North Caucasus, Dagestan among them, as an area where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note documents systematic campaigns by Chechen and other North Caucasus authorities between 2017 and 2024 involving abduction, torture and extrajudicial killing, and it assesses trans people and visible advocates specifically rather than treating the risk as confined to gay and lesbian residents.

Global Affairs Canada advises against all travel to Russia. Its advisory flags frequent terrorist attacks in the republics of Chechnya, Dagestan, Ingushetia and Stavropol Krai, states that entry to certain areas and regions requires special permission from the Ministry of the Interior, and warns of violence targeting 2SLGBTQI+ persons, naming the North Caucasus republics of Chechnya and Dagestan in particular.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, who works in exile, told the Human Rights House Foundation that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus. The campaigns documented in the Home Office note run from 2017 to 2024; no later incident in Dagestan or the wider North Caucasus is documented in this inventory.
tangentialFactors:
Isteev's assessment to the Human Rights House Foundation is that the situation for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus worsens year on year, which places the 2017 to 2024 campaign period at the low end of the documented trajectory rather than its peak.

The Canadian advisory singles out the North Caucasus republics of Chechnya and Dagestan for 2SLGBTQI+ violence instead of treating that risk as uniform across Russia, and separately flags frequent terrorist attacks in Dagestan, Chechnya, Ingushetia and Stavropol Krai. The terrorism designation is an adjacent security condition that shapes the overall environment in which an LGBT+ visitor would be moving.
localsOnly:
Support for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus is delivered from outside the region: David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS works in exile, and his account to the Human Rights House Foundation is that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families.

For residents, exposure carries a family dimension that a visitor moving through the region does not share in the same form: forced return to families is named as a consequence of private existence being discovered, alongside violence and detention.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Dagestan-specific documentation appears in this inventory on document screening at regional entry points, on bathroom or facility access, on local access to gender-affirming care, or on any dated trans-specific killing within Dagestan itself. The persecution assessment and the campaign record are made at North Caucasus level, and the inventory does not break them down by republic.

The Canadian advisory states that entry to certain areas and regions requires special permission from the Ministry of the Interior but does not specify which areas of Dagestan fall under that requirement; which districts are restricted, and how the permission is obtained, remain unresolved on this evidence.

Whether the Home Office persecution finding has been tested in an asylum appeal concerning Dagestan specifically is not sourced here, and no Dagestan-specific court decision on LGBT+ or trans claims is documented in this inventory.
